hints: Look closely at the position of the -OH group in each alcohol and what is attached to that same carbon.
Notice that 3-methylbutan-2-ol contains the group $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ while 2-methylbutan-1-ol does not.
Remember which test gives a yellow precipitate only with that specific group, while leaving other alcohols unchanged.
walkthrough:
**Classify the two alcohols**

First, let's see what kind of alcohols we have. 2-methylbutan-1-ol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$, so the -OH is on a carbon with only one other carbon. That is a primary alcohol.

3-methylbutan-2-ol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_3$, so the -OH is on a carbon with two other carbons. That is a secondary alcohol, and importantly it has a $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ unit.

**Think about what makes a visible difference**

We need a reagent that reacts differently with these two structures. Many general alcohol tests, like effervescence or steamy fumes, will happen with both primary and secondary alcohols, so they cannot tell them apart.

**Recall the iodoform test**

Alkaline iodine, $\text{I}_2$ in $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, is the tri-iodomethane (iodoform) test. It gives a very distinctive yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$ only with molecules containing either $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)R + 4OH}^- + 3\text{I}_2 \rightarrow \text{CHI}_3\text{(s, yellow)} + \text{RCOO}^- + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Apply it to our pair**

3-methylbutan-2-ol has the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ group, so it gives the yellow precipitate. 2-methylbutan-1-ol does not have this group, so the brown iodine colour simply fades with no precipitate. The visible results are clearly different, so this is our reagent.

options.A: Sodium reacts with all alcohols to give hydrogen gas: $2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$. Both a primary and a secondary alcohol will fizz in the same way, so there is no visible difference.
options.B: Alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ is the iodoform test. Only 3-methylbutan-2-ol contains $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$, so it forms yellow $\text{CHI}_3$ precipitate, while 2-methylbutan-1-ol gives no precipitate. This gives clearly different observations.
options.C: $\text{PCl}_5$ reacts with any alcohol with -OH to give steamy white fumes of $\text{HCl}$: $\text{ROH} + \text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{RCl} + \text{POCl}_3 + \text{HCl}$. Both alcohols do this identically, so it cannot distinguish them.
options.D: Acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ is an oxidising agent that is decolourised from purple to colourless by both alcohols. The primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde then a carboxylic acid, and the secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone. The visible change is the same for both.
